Read More, Reason Deeper: Latent Workspaces for Long-Sequence Recommendation

Renzhi Wu Affiliation: Meta MRS    Li Sheng Affiliation: Meta MRS    Zikun Cui Affiliation: Meta MRS    Junjie Yang Affiliation: Meta MRS    Tai Guo Affiliation: Meta MRS    Keke Zhai Affiliation: Meta MRS    Yan Li Affiliation: Meta MRS    Jerry Fu Affiliation: Facebook Discovery    Nipun Mathur Affiliation: Meta MRS    Sri Reddy Affiliation: Meta MRS    Hong Li Affiliation: Meta MRS
Abstract

Long-sequence recommendation can improve along two axes: evidence scaling exposes longer histories, while reasoning scaling adds layers that interpret that evidence for a candidate. Existing models couple them: sequence encoders propagate every added event through depth, whereas one-shot selection prevents later layers from revisiting omitted evidence. We introduce the Latent Workspace Ranker (LWR), which keeps typed evidence in persistent banks and propagates a fixed-size candidate-local workspace. Each layer rereads the banks from its evolving workspace and archives compact post-interaction state, allowing history length and reasoning depth to grow independently. We compare four architectures across various history–depth configurations using evidence scaling at fixed depth, reasoning scaling at fixed 10K history, and their joint compute-efficient frontier. LWR leads all families at long histories, continues improving with reasoning compute, and converts additional training compute into quality gains at the fastest fitted rate on the joint frontier. At 10K history, it improves NE by 0.19% over HSTU while using 69.6% fewer forward GFLOP/request. It also outperforms existing baselines on two billion-scale ranking surfaces. These results show that separating addressable evidence from propagated state makes reading more and reasoning deeper independently controllable and jointly useful.

††date: October 29, 2026††correspondence: Renzhi Wu at renzhiwu@meta.com††Keywords: Long-sequence recommendation, Recommender systems

1 Introduction

Sequential recommendation models can typically be improved in two ways: More events expose more evidence about a user’s interests; more layers let a model reinterpret that evidence as its representation of a candidate evolves. We call these directions evidence scaling and reasoning scaling. A useful architecture for long-sequence recommendation should control them independently and benefit from both: reading more history should not enlarge the state that every layer transforms, and adding layers should not cut off access to the original history.

Yet current designs couple these axes. Sequence encoders keep event representations active across layers (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Zhai et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2026); lengthening history therefore expands work throughout the stack. Target-aware pooling (Zhou et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019) and retrieval-based rankers (Pi et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2023; Si et al., 2024) bound active state by summarizing evidence before feature interaction, but this makes evidence selection effectively one-shot. Once an event is omitted, later layers cannot recover it. This matters because the useful evidence can change during reasoning: an early representation may match a candidate to a stable preference, while a later one emphasizes the current session. Existing designs thus face a structural choice: carry more evidence through every layer, or let deeper reasoning operate on evidence chosen only once.

Latent workspaces decouple the two axes. We introduce the Latent Workspace Ranker (LWR), which separates what the model can read from what it must carry. Typed history, request/user context, and matched events remain in persistent external banks. Candidate features initialize a fixed-size workspace that alone moves through the stack. Evidence scaling increases bank cardinality and read length, whereas reasoning scaling increases the number of workspace layers. These are separate structural controls: changing either does not enlarge the representation governed by the other.

This separation is useful only if later layers can use the retained evidence differently. Each LWR layer therefore Coordinates its workspace, uses the result to Query each bank, Rereads the returned evidence, and Interacts the responses with ranking features (Figure 1). Non-final layers write a few condensate tokens to an archive. Because both the workspace and archive evolve, a later layer can formulate a candidate-specific follow-up read from earlier results while still accessing the original evidence. Longer histories provide more addressable evidence; deeper stacks ask better-informed questions of it.

Three curves expose two-axis scaling. The central test is whether the separated axes produce useful gains rather than merely configurable knobs. We evaluate four architectures on a grid of history lengths and reasoning depths, then read that grid in three ways. The evidence curve holds depth fixed and asks whether longer history helps. The reasoning curve holds history fixed and asks whether added reasoning continues to pay off relative to its training compute. The joint curve removes both restrictions: among all history–depth combinations, it traces the configurations that are not beaten in both compute and NE. It therefore asks how well each architecture allocates a compute budget between reading more and reasoning deeper, rather than forcing both axes to increase in lockstep.

LWR leads all four families in the long-history regime, continues improving throughout the fixed-history reasoning sweep, and has the steepest joint compute-frontier trend. Its reducible normalized entropy (NE), the normalized-log-loss error remaining above a fitted floor, falls fastest as training compute grows along that frontier. At 10K history, LWR achieves a statistically significant 0.19% NE improvement over HSTU while using 69.6% fewer forward GFLOP/request. In addition, LWR improves critical-task NE by 0.08–0.09% over the existing baseline on Surface 1 and improves NE by 0.15–0.30% over HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024) on Surface 2.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    An architecture for decoupled scaling: LWR keeps evidence in persistent typed banks while a fixed-size candidate-local workspace moves through depth. Repeated reads preserve access to original evidence, and a condensate archive carries compact intermediate reasoning across layers.

  • •

    Three complementary scaling curves: We isolate evidence scaling at fixed depth and reasoning scaling at fixed history, then define joint scaling as the compute-efficient envelope of the full history–depth grid. LWR benefits strongly from longer histories, continues improving with deeper reasoning, and has the steepest joint-frontier trend.

  • •

    Billion-scale quality and compute efficiency: LWR outperforms existing baselines on two ranking surfaces. At 10K history it improves NE by 0.19% over HSTU with 69.6% fewer forward GFLOP/request.

2 Related Work

Sequential recommenders encode history with recurrent (Zhou et al., 2019), self-attentive (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019), or generative sequence models (Zhai et al., 2024). Long-history methods restrict the active evidence through external memory (Pi et al., 2019), target-aware activation (Zhou et al., 2018), retrieval (Pi et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2023; Si et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), or sampling (Cao et al., 2022); efficient long-context models instead reduce sequence-processing cost through sparsity or IO-aware kernels (Dai et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Kitaev et al., 2020; Dao et al., 2022). These methods make longer histories practical, but generally do not separate the evidence retained from the state propagated through later ranking interactions.

Bounded-latent models provide complementary ingredients: Set Transformer uses inducing points (Lee et al., 2019), Perceiver alternates cross-attention and latent processing (Jaegle et al., 2021; Jaegle et al., 2022), and memory networks repeatedly read external state (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015). LWR adapts these ideas to ranking with source-specific queries, explicit FM/deep-cross interactions (Cheng et al., 2016; Rendle, 2010; Guo et al., 2017; Lian et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Song et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019), and compressed post-interaction state shared across layers. The contribution is their composition for decoupled evidence and reasoning scaling, together with its long-sequence evaluation.

Most directly, SlimPer (Wang et al., 2026) queries raw user-side tokens while iteratively refining a compact knowledge base. LWR instead separates persistent typed evidence, a candidate-local workspace, and an all-prior archive of compressed post-interaction states.

3 Latent Workspace Ranker

3.1 Architecture overview

LWR separates persistent evidence from compact propagated state. For request rr and candidate ii, let xr,ix_{r,i} be candidate context, fr,if_{r,i} a dense interaction projection, and {Srhist,Srctx,Sr,isim}\{S_{r}^{\rm hist},S_{r}^{\rm ctx},S_{r,i}^{\rm sim}\} the typed evidence banks. We use 𝒮={hist,ctx,sim}\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{hist},\mathrm{ctx},\mathrm{sim}\} to index them and SsS^{s} when request and candidate indices are clear. History and request context are request-shared; matched events are candidate-private.

At layer ll, the propagated state is a candidate-local workspace Zl∈𝐑K×dZ_{l}\in\mathbf{R}^{K\times d} and an archive C<l=[c0;…;cl−1]C_{<l}=[c_{0};\ldots;c_{l-1}] of completed layer states, with C<0=∅C_{<0}=\emptyset. Here KK is the workspace slot count, dd the hidden width, and each of the DD layers maps ZlZ_{l} to Zl+1Z_{l+1}. Figure 1 shows the four steps: Coordinate the workspace, Query each source, Reread its evidence, and Interact the responses with ranking features. Each source receives rsr_{s} queries, and every non-final layer appends qcq_{c} condensate tokens to the archive. The following subsections define these operations.

The same structure exposes two scaling controls. Evidence scaling changes Ns=|Ss|N_{s}=|S^{s}|, while reasoning scaling changes DD. Keeping KK, rsr_{s}, and qcq_{c} bounded prevents either axis from enlarging the state controlled by the other. Source reads still scale with NsN_{s} and repeat across DD; LWR decouples state growth, not total computation.

3.2 Coordinate: evolve a compact workspace

The initial workspace combines candidate-derived and learned slots:

Z0\displaystyle Z_{0} =[Q0;M0]=[ϕcand​(xr,i);ΘM],\displaystyle=[Q_{0};M_{0}]=[\phi_{\rm cand}(x_{r,i});\Theta_{M}], K\displaystyle K =nQ+nM,\displaystyle=n_{Q}+n_{M},
Z¯l\displaystyle\bar{Z}_{l} =WSAl⁡(Norml⁡(Zl)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{WSA}_{l}(\operatorname{Norm}_{l}(Z_{l})). (1)

Here ϕcand\phi_{\rm cand} maps candidate context to nQn_{Q} slots, ΘM∈𝐑nM×d\Theta_{M}\in\mathbf{R}^{n_{M}\times d} contains nMn_{M} learned slots, and Q0=ϕcand​(xr,i)Q_{0}=\phi_{\rm cand}(x_{r,i}), M0=ΘMM_{0}=\Theta_{M}. The learned bank is broadcast to every candidate and supplies content-independent working capacity. Norml\operatorname{Norm}_{l} and WSAl\operatorname{WSA}_{l} denote the layer’s normalization and workspace self-attention. QQ and MM describe initialization provenance only; subsequent operations mix all slots into mutable state. Unlike a fixed multi-interest bank (Li et al., 2019), learned slots need not retain static semantic roles. Coordinate applies normalized, dense, non-causal self-attention over the KK slots of one candidate.

3.3 Query: form source-specific requests

The tokenizer TlT_{l} converts the coordinated workspace Z¯l\bar{Z}_{l}, prior condensates C<lC_{<l}, and layer-specific learned prior tokens PlP_{l} into one bounded query bank Uls∈𝐑rs×dU_{l}^{s}\in\mathbf{R}^{r_{s}\times d} per source ss:

Ul=Tl​([Z¯l;C<l;Pl]),{Uls}s=Split⁡(Ul).U_{l}=T_{l}([\bar{Z}_{l};C_{<l};P_{l}]),\qquad\{U_{l}^{s}\}_{s}=\operatorname{Split}(U_{l}). (2)

Here UlU_{l} is the combined query bank, and Split\operatorname{Split} partitions it into the prescribed rsr_{s} queries for each source. Because the workspace and archive change with depth, so do the queries: an early layer can ask a broad history question, while a later layer can ask a candidate-specific follow-up informed by completed interactions. Query is the bridge between the two scaling axes: larger banks provide more addressable evidence, while added layers generate new requests from the evolving reasoning state.

Separate banks preserve source identity instead of forcing heterogeneous evidence into one undifferentiated query. Query construction retains a static token-mixing arm and adds a content-dependent arm whose output projection is initialized at zero. The initial function is therefore preserved while the adaptive path receives gradients from the first update.

3.4 Reread: access persistent typed evidence

Each UlsU_{l}^{s} rereads source SsS^{s} through cross-attention. Packed history and request/user context are request-scoped, while matched events are candidate-scoped. Grouped offsets let all candidates address their request’s shared banks without copying them; candidate offsets keep private reads from crossing examples. The original typed sources remain available at every layer, so later computation need not accept an irrevocable early summary: Rls=Attn⁡(Uls,Ss,Ss)R_{l}^{s}=\operatorname{Attn}(U_{l}^{s},S^{s},S^{s}) where Attn\operatorname{Attn} denotes multi-head cross-attention and Rls∈𝐑rs×dR_{l}^{s}\in\mathbf{R}^{r_{s}\times d} is the response from source ss.

This step is related to multi-hop external memory (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015) and iterative latent reads (Jaegle et al., 2021; Jaegle et al., 2022), but it retains source ownership and places an explicit ranking interaction after retrieval. Bounded queries make the propagated state independent of source length, not the read itself: a source of length NsN_{s} with rsr_{s} queries still contributes O⁡(rs​Ns​d)O(r_{s}N_{s}d) attention work.

3.5 Interact: update ranking state

The block FlF_{l} is a ranking-specific Cross/FM interaction over the coordinated workspace, retrieved source responses, earlier condensates, and dense feature: Zl+1=Fl​([Z¯l;{Rls}s;C<l],fr,i).Z_{l+1}=F_{l}([\bar{Z}_{l};\{R_{l}^{s}\}_{s};C_{<l}],f_{r,i}). This keeps evidence access distinct from explicit feature crossing, following the FM and deep-cross lineage (Rendle, 2010; Guo et al., 2017; Lian et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Song et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019). Its output is again Zl+1∈𝐑K×dZ_{l+1}\in\mathbf{R}^{K\times d}, so deep candidate reasoning does not inherit source cardinality. The final layer emits a fixed-width representation to the PLE multi-task module and its task heads.

3.6 Stacking layers through a condensate archive

Every non-final layer applies a learned compressor κl:𝐑K×d→𝐑qc×d\kappa_{l}:\mathbf{R}^{K\times d}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}^{q_{c}\times d} to its post-interaction workspace and appends the resulting qcq_{c} tokens to the archive:

cl=κl(Zl+1),C<l+1=[C<l;cl](l<D−1).c_{l}=\kappa_{l}(Z_{l+1}),\qquad C_{<l+1}=[C_{<l};c_{l}]\quad(l<D-1). (3)

A condensate therefore records how that layer combined candidate state, retrieved evidence, and ranking features; it is not another copy of source tokens. Thus cl∈𝐑qc×dc_{l}\in\mathbf{R}^{q_{c}\times d} and C<l∈𝐑l​qc×dC_{<l}\in\mathbf{R}^{lq_{c}\times d}. Layer ll receives all earlier condensates C<lC_{<l} in both Query and Interact. It can reread an original source, consult a compact record of prior decisions, or combine both paths.

This all-prior connection gives later layers direct access to every completed stage without propagating full intermediate activations. It differs from uncompressed dense concatenation (Huang et al., 2017) and temporal compression across sequence segments (Rae et al., 2020): LWR compresses state across network depth. Reasoning scaling increases DD; if each layer writes qcq_{c} tokens, layer ll reads l​qclq_{c} archive tokens, and the stored candidate-local state is O⁡((K+D​qc)​d)O((K+Dq_{c})d). Evidence scaling changes the source lengths used only in Reread; the large banks remain external and can stay request-shared.

The four-step layer and archive together create two recurrent paths: original evidence is revisited across sequence length, while compressed decisions are revisited across network depth.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup and metrics

We first compare LWR with existing reference rankers on two surfaces, then use one history–depth grid to isolate evidence scaling, reasoning scaling, and their best joint use of compute.

Data and hardware. Each model trains on three consecutive days of online data (30–50 billion examples, depending on the surface) and evaluates on the following day. Runs use mixed precision on 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs on an internal training platform with customized memory and throughput kernels.

Settings. Overall comparisons use 3K histories, with HSTU as the Surface 2 reference and a existing baseline as the Surface 1 reference. LWR uses five layers, 76 workspace slots , 24 queries per typed source, and four condensates per non-final layer; its 2048-dimensional output feeds the unchanged PLE module.

Scaling protocol. Evidence scaling uses 12 history lengths from 2K to 65K at base depth. Reasoning scaling uses nine depths at fixed 10K history and plots each run at its measured total training compute. Joint scaling takes the nondominated lower envelope of all 117 configurations per family: a point is retained only if no other point has both no worse NE and no greater compute, with one strict improvement. It therefore measures the best allocation of compute between history and depth.

Metrics. Normalized entropy (NE) (He et al., 2014) is binary log loss divided by empirical label entropy; lower is better. We report NE reductions as 100​(NEbase−NELWR)100(\mathrm{NE}_{\rm base}-\mathrm{NE}_{\rm LWR}), and improvements above 0.03% are statistically significant under the surface-level protocol. Surface 1 instead reports critical-task p-diff, where negative is better; the two surface metrics are not combined. Forward GFLOP/request measures the 3K, 5K, and 10K headline slice, while total forward-plus-backward training compute defines the reasoning and joint curves. Figure 2 reports reducible NE, NE−E\mathrm{NE}-E: Figures 2(a) and (b) share one floor to preserve raw-NE ordering, while Figure 2(c) fits one floor per architecture to compare frontier slopes.

4.2 Overall results on two ranking surfaces

Table 1 shows consistent gains across both surfaces. LWR improves Surface 2 train and evaluation NE by 0.15–0.30%, all above the 0.03% significance threshold, and yields NE diff of -0.08% globally and -0.09% regionally on Surface 1. The metrics are surface-specific, so we do not pool them.

4.3 Evidence, reasoning, and joint scaling

Evidence scaling: read more at fixed depth. Figure 2(a) isolates evidence scaling by fixing the base reasoning depth. At 3K, 5K, and 10K history, LWR improves NE over HSTU by 0.11%, 0.12%, and 0.19% while reducing measured forward GFLOP/request by 19.6%, 48.2%, and 69.6%; all three NE gains exceed the 0.03% significance threshold. At 10K, Internal Baseline 2 is only 0.01% better, below the threshold, but uses 136.28 rather than 52.69 GFLOP/request. Across the full 2K–65K sweep, LWR starts behind Internal Baseline 1 and leads all four families from 12K onward, showing that its advantage grows with available evidence.

Reasoning scaling: reason deeper at fixed evidence. Figure 2(b) isolates reasoning scaling by holding history at 10,240 events and varying relative depth from 0.5×0.5\times to 8×8\times. All four families improve monotonically, and LWR improves NE by 0.41% as deeper workspace layers extract more value from unchanged evidence. Total training compute, rather than nominal depth, makes this a quality-per-reasoning-compute comparison. At 8×8\times depth, LWR outperforms HSTU and Internal Baseline 1; Internal Baseline 2 is 0.02% better, below the significance threshold, but uses 3.5 times as much training compute.

Joint scaling: spend compute on either axis. Figure 2(c) takes the compute-efficient envelope of every history–depth combination, measuring the best quality when compute may be spent on either axis. Following neural scaling studies (Hestness et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), we fit NE=Em+Am​C−αm\mathrm{NE}=E_{m}+A_{m}C^{-\alpha_{m}} to each frontier, where αm\alpha_{m} measures how quickly reducible NE falls under the best allocation. LWR has the steepest frontier exponent: α=0.845\alpha=0.845{}, versus 0.558, 0.424, and 0.599 for HSTU and Internal Baselines 1 and 2. Figure 2(c) fits EmE_{m} separately for each family, so vertical position represents reducible scaling behavior, not raw-NE ordering. Together, the three curves show that LWR benefits from more evidence, deeper reasoning, and their joint allocation.

5 Conclusion

Latent Workspace Ranker decouples evidence scaling from reasoning scaling: persistent typed banks retain long histories, while a compact workspace repeatedly reads them and carries state across layers. It outperforms HSTU and a existing baseline on two billion-scale ranking surfaces. At fixed depth, LWR leads all evaluated families from 12K through 65K history; at fixed history, it continues improving with reasoning compute; and across all 468 history–depth configurations, it has the steepest fitted compute-efficient frontier. Together, these results show that long-sequence recommenders can read more and reason deeper without coupling both forms of capacity to the same expanding sequence state.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
